cards.title: Third conditional
points: It talks about a past that **did not** happen — and the result that therefore did not happen either.
Fact: I didn't leave early, so I missed the train.
Unreal: If I **had left** earlier, I **would have** caught the train.
You use it to explain, to regret, or to blame.

rows: I didn't leave early. I missed the train.
If I **had left** earlier, I would have caught the train.
If she **had studied**, she would have passed.
We didn't know. We didn't help.
If we **had known**, we would have helped.

cards.title: The two halves
points: Both halves use a past participle — the same form as the present perfect.
**had** never changes for person: I had, she had, they had.

cards.title: Either half can come first

rows: If we **had known**, we would have helped.
I **would have** come if I had known.
Would you have accepted if they had offered more?

points: The meaning does not change with the order. Only the comma does.
In a question, **would** moves to the front: Would he have come…?

cards.title: Second or third?

rows: If I had time, I would help.
If I **had had** time, I would have helped.

points: Second: it could still be different. Third: it cannot — it is over.
**had had** looks odd and is correct: had (the conditional) + had (the verb).

cards.title: Common mistakes
points: Czech puts *by* in both halves, so **would** wants to jump into the if-half. It cannot.
**would have** is always followed by a past participle, never the plain verb.

cards.title: Negatives

rows: If the flight **had not** been delayed, we would have landed on time.
If I had taken a taxi, I would **not have** been late.

points: **not** sits between would and have, not on the far side of have.
